I am an accomplished Product Management expert and instructor. After working 15 years in small and FAANG companies, I moved on to helping others excel in their product career. My online courses were attended by over 20,000 people, and hundreds of them got a new job thanks to my help. I am also a co-author of a best-selling book, "Next-Gen Product Manager," and a successful live event speaker.

I'm currently focusing on growing my Newsletter, tending to live cohort training I lead with Aakash Gupta, a fellow product creator, and growing as a speaker and in-house trainer for companies that seek my help.

If you need my help, make sure to contact me today on LinkedIn or email me at [email protected].

Are you afraid of falling behind with AI usage as a Product Manager? Here are 𝟮𝟭𝟴 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗱𝘂𝗰𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗦𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀 and how to install and use them:

Let's be honest: Most of the AI news is either fear-mongering or pushing hype. Chasing every release is a great way to feel busy and learn nothing. 

What actually moves the needle is smaller: a few tools that quietly give you back an hour a week on the work you already repeat.
 
So I did the boring part for you. I went through 218 Claude skills built for product managers, wrote a plain-English description for each one, and put them all in one place.
 
A few honest words before you dive in.
 
This is a catalogue, not a leaderboard. Some are brilliant. Some are niche. And not every skill will fit you. 

What's gold for one PM is noise for another, depending on your company and how your team works. Try one on real work and keep what earns its place.
 
They won't replace you - they will help you step up and push your productivity through the roof. 
 
Five free ones I'd use every week:
 
• PRD Generator by Lucky Bajaj: a solid first draft instead of a blank page
• User Interview Analyzer by Ron Yang: turns a pile of notes into themes and quotes
• Status Update Writer by Aakash Gupta: the same update, retuned for execs, engineers, and partners
• Prioritize Features by Pawel Huryn : forces you to defend the tradeoff out loud
• Idea Validator by Aakash Gupta: pokes holes in an idea before a stakeholder does
 
How to install one, for people who'd rather not touch anything technical. No terminal, no code, nothing on your machine. If you can upload a file, you can do this:
 
1. In Claude, go to Settings > Capabilities and switch on "Code execution and file creation."
2. Go to Customize > Skills, then toggle on anything you want to try.
3. To add a free skill from the list: download its folder, put it in a ZIP (the folder goes inside the ZIP, not the loose files), then in Customize > Skills hit "+" and upload it.
4. To use it, just describe your task like normal, or type "/" and pick the skill. Claude takes it from there.
 
One rule for peace of mind: only add skills from people you trust.
 
The full list of all 218, with descriptions and links, is here:  

https://lnkd.in/d8Vd-HWm
 
Try one and tell me which one stuck. I read every reply.
 
So, what's already in your daily PM stack?

Let me know in the comments

Have you ever seen an ALMOST completed new feature that had its release dragging on for weeks? Here is how to prevent this:

I must say, nothing feels more frustrating in the Product Manager life when week after week you have to report that the feature promised weeks ago is almost completed, but (pick your poison):

• Translations are not ready
• Design is not adapted properly
• Key team members are missing
• We are still sorting the final bugs
• We can't release during the holidays
• Tracking isn't what it's supposed to be
• We're waiting for a partner API to work
• We need the other team to make their release first
• We got feedback from a key CEO, uhm, stakeholder, and need to address it before the release.

Probably something to do with President Trump, Godzilla attack, or new GTA game release should also make this list.

Not to mention a brief ask to follow me and subscribe to my free newsletter: https://lnkd.in/ddD_FU5q

Regardless..

It's your ass that delivers the bad news.

The delay has your voice and face.

You are the target of (well-deserved) frustration (that you share) and have to provide the explanation.

Yet... You can't really do anything about it. You are, in a way, as much of a spectator as the people upset with you about the very same delay.

Perhaps there is something you can do?

Well, the initial instinct from the team is usually to give any project more prep time and risk assessment to have the development and release be carried out as a well-planned process.

This is a waterfall.

This doesn't work. 

This is why we have Agile Scrum - to adjust on the fly to any issues and maximize delivering value. 

Even then, the 5% of work missing to get something live can drag on for weeks.

So, how to damage control pre-emptively?

1) Avoid release dates; operate on quarters - While this is hard, and stakeholders will push back hard, it is still the single most effective way to reduce artificial pressure and false certainty. Quarters give you room to absorb reality.

2) Define “release ready” upfront:  Translations, tracking, legal, and  partners. If it is not done, the feature is not done. Almost done is a lie we tell ourselves.

3) Ship thinner: Cut scope aggressively so the last 5 percent is not a minefield of dependencies.

4) Treat release as a feature.  Plan it, own it, review it. Not as an afterthought.

5) Assess risks week to week. A broken release pipeline usually doesn't happen overnight. Fix it before it extends the final 5% to infinity, or at least include it in your comms.

Remember, delays are rarely about bad teams. They are about pretending uncertainty does not exist or can be controlled. 

It does, and it can't.

So, did you have a release that took forever to push through the finish line?

Let me know in the comments.

Are Product Managers being naive when we say we serve our users? Is it really all about the money? Here's the truth:

We, the Product Managers, are all about creating value. That will most often translate into making the product profitable or ensuring a high company valuation to keep the shareholders happy. 

The sad truth is that only once that is met, and not always, can the product management idealism come into consideration. Stuff like chasing better NPS, reacting to user feedback, running Jobs To Be Done workshops, mood boards, journey maps, emotional maps, heatmap analysis, usability testing, and accessibility reviews. You know, the whole user-centric toolbox.”

"Bart, you're mad; those are just basic PM tools," you might say.

They are.

But they are forgotten the moment the profits are not there (and where they should be)

Then, it's a rush to get more profits, whatever means necessary, regardless of the previous checks and boundaries. It's all hands on board to "fix" the monetization.

And... why not?

Brief ask, as an interlude:  

Don't miss any of my posts: 
Hit that follow button and sign up for my newsletter: https://lnkd.in/dxmBqj3Q

Back to the post.

It pays the salaries and gets the business and product going.

When you are at war, you don't invest in handicap ramps and social benefits; you build tanks. 

However, what I am on about today is an observation that very often companies will swing from one extreme ("We care primarily about our customers and quality of the product") to another ("Where can we find more cash to milk our users?"), sometimes without seeing actual significant losses. 

That leaves me with a question: 
What should a Great Product Manager do?

Answer: Never put yourself in a situation where you operate on such extremes. 

The process should always involve providing the most value possible as a Product Manager. This can only be achieved by having backlog and roadmap inputs from a diverse pool of sources (user and stakeholder requests), prioritizing them against one another on just terms, WHILE keeping in mind your ROI (Return on Investment) and broader company strategy and goals.

That also means dropping the ‘we serve users’ charade when it becomes a shield, and reminding other PMs and stakeholders that we’re running a business, not a charity.

That also means pointing out when greed takes over, and the company forgets that it was built to solve a problem and earn from the solution provided. However, this solution needs to be always built with users and their voices in mind, not their wallets. 

Because the best products don’t just earn money from users. They earn money because they serve users well.

Bring value by serving users. But don’t become a slave- not to the money, and not to the users.

Have you ever been a slave to either?

Let me know in the comments.

#productmanagement #productmanager #usercentricity

"Talk to the users" is the most ignored product principle. Here's how to easily present the user's perspective to your team:

In an ideal world, I would always want my features to be verified through the discovery process. 

That is bound to help me direct the development process the right way to better fit users' needs, and will highlight any gaps or wrong assumptions that I have made while figuring out my next step.

It is no secret, though, that discovery takes a lot of time. The delay usually comes from actually finding the right users to interview, not to mention having time and resources to get the recruitment started.

Fortunately, there's another way that you can now consider.

Synthesia, the partner of this post, has something that can help. Synthesia is an all-in-one AI Video platform for business. It allows you to create studio-quality videos with AI avatars and voiceovers in 160+ languages.

And those avatars, or "users" are your key to quick user interviews. Their new Brief Roleplay Sessions feature allows you to basically summon a number of users to interview live, whether that's in private or in front of your team during a refinement session, and ask the questions directly. 

The user vault is there to talk to the team, share their perspective, and allow everyone in the room to better understand how a real user might react to what you're building.

Well, of course, "users"-based discovery efforts will always be an approximation of the real deal. However, you can build those avatars for role-playing sessions based on the previous discovery sessions and your user personas that you've identified in the past for a product. 

That will give AI enough context to create virtual people that will provide you with the fresh and direct user perspective you seek in order to develop better products.

So, to summarize the benefits of this approach:
• Instant sessions and feedback - you talk to your "users" when and where you need them to be. Not when the recruitment process is done weeks later.
• "Users" that don't get tired - humans might be bad sparring partners. AI will patiently answer every question with the same high energy.
• Reduced costs - "here and now" means it's way cheaper than organizing real user interviews. 
• Whole team has the same access - you don't present other people's findings to your team; they can ask their questions themselves, directly!
• Reusability - you can talk to the same "user" multiple times without having past sessions impact newer ones.
  
Remember, avatar-based discovery is an approximation, not a substitute. 
  
If you want to see how the Brief Roleplay Sessions feature works, it's worth a look: 

https://lnkd.in/d33aghu7
  
Was there a time a user interview changed the course of a planned update?
